common_name: Lewis Palmer Lungwort (Vivid Blue Silver-Spotted Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring or just after flowering, replanting promptly in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this long-grown English cultivar is valued for flowers that open a clean, saturated blue rather than shifting through the pink-to-blue range typical of most lungworts.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the coarse, silver-spotted leaves resist scorch better than solid-green forms. Funnel-shaped flowers open a true, vivid blue in earliest spring atop bristly stems, holding their color longer than many pulmonarias whose blooms fade quickly to lavender. The broad, tapering leaves expand through late spring into a dense, weed-suppressing clump that persists as attractive groundcover well after bloom. Water during dry spells and shear tattered summer foliage to encourage fresh, well-spotted new leaves for fall.

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or right after flowering and replant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Dora Bielefeld holds its coral-pink flower color rather than aging toward blue, giving a warmer-toned display than most spotted lungworts.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool through summer. Clusters of salmon-pink, funnel-shaped flowers open in early spring and stay pink rather than shifting toward blue as the season progresses, pairing well with lungworts of the classic pink-and-blue type nearby. Broad, softly hairy leaves are heavily marked with silvery-white spots and expand after bloom into a dense clump that shades out early weeds. Divide every three to four years to maintain vigor, and water during summer dry spells since thin foliage wilts quickly under drought stress.

planting.note: Divide in early spring or after flowering and replant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this historic selection, raised at Sir Frederick Stern's chalk garden at Highdown in Sussex, tolerates lean, alkaline soils better than many modern hybrids.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, where it adapts more readily to chalky or alkaline conditions than many newer pulmonaria cultivars. Nodding clusters of blue-violet flowers open in early spring on bristly stems just as the narrow, sparsely spotted leaves are emerging. Foliage lengthens through late spring into a modest, tidy clump that is less flashy than heavily silvered modern cultivars but reliably floriferous and long-lived once established. Keep soil evenly moist during the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to renew flowering vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the leathery, holly-like leaflets are sharply spined along the margins, so site it away from paths where bare hands or legs might brush against it.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, where the stiff evergreen foliage provides winter structure that deciduous epimediums cannot. Epimedium ilicifolium is named for its unusually spiny, holly-shaped leaflets, which stay glossy dark green year-round and give the clump a distinctly textured, almost shrubby look. In spring, wiry stems lift small clusters of pale creamy-yellow flowers with short spurs just above the spined foliage, offering a quiet contrast to the bold leaves. Once established it tolerates the dry shade found beneath mature trees; comb out any winter-damaged leaves in late winter before new spurred flowers appear, wearing gloves given the sharp leaf margins.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Guizhou and Sichuan woodlander is named for its unusually crowded flower sprays and benefits from a season or two to settle in before it flowers at full density.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, watering regularly the first year while the clump establishes. Epimedium myrianthum takes its name, meaning 'many-flowered,' from the crowded, branching sprays it produces in mid-spring, each carrying far more small white flowers than most Chinese epimedium species. Semi-evergreen leaflets emerge with a light bronze tint before settling into leathery, deep green foliage that persists through much of the winter in milder zones. Once established the clump tolerates the dry shade beneath deciduous trees; groom out tattered old leaves in late winter so the dense flower sprays are not obscured.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Yunnan woodland species has thin, membranous leaflets that scorch easily in wind or sun and are best given a sheltered spot.

directions: Site in a sheltered spot with humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, protected from drying wind that can tatter the thin leaves. Epimedium membranaceum produces broad, thin-textured leaflets that emerge with reddish-bronze mottling in spring before turning soft green for summer. In mid-spring, arching stems carry loose sprays of white to pale purple flowers with slender, elegant spurs held well clear of the foliage. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season, since the delicate leaves wilt faster in drought than the more leathery-leaved epimedium species.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this compact Sichuan-Guizhou limestone species prefers a lean, sharply drained site over the richer soils suited to larger epimediums.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, well-drained soil enriched lightly with leaf mold, in partial or full shade, mimicking the limestone crevices of its native Sichuan and Guizhou range. Named for the Japanese botanist Mikinori Ogisu, who collected extensively among Chinese epimediums, this dwarf species forms a low, tight mound of small, neatly heart-shaped leaflets. In spring, short stems hold dainty white to pale pink flowers just above the foliage, giving a delicate look well suited to a shaded rock garden or trough. Avoid heavy, waterlogged soil, since good drainage matters more to this compact species than to larger, more vigorously spreading epimediums.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; native to Hebei and Shanxi in northern China, this is among the most cold-hardy epimediums and tolerates colder winters than most Chinese species in cultivation.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade; because it hails from the colder mountains of Hebei and Shanxi, this species handles harsher winters than most Chinese epimediums without special protection. Deciduous, arrow-shaped leaflets emerge with a light bronze cast in spring and mature to clean green through summer, dying back fully at the first hard freeze. In mid-spring, wiry stems lift small sprays of soft yellow flowers with short spurs just above the new foliage. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a modest, well-mannered patch, making it a good choice for gardeners in colder climates who want a true species epimedium rather than a hardier hybrid.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the leaflets have a distinctive flattened, truncated base rather than the tapering heart shape typical of most epimediums.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, where the clump spreads slowly into a tidy patch of textured foliage. Epimedium truncatum is named for the flattened, truncated base of its leaflets, which gives the semi-evergreen foliage a squared-off look distinct from the heart-shaped leaves of most epimediums. In spring, slender stems carry loose clusters of small white flowers with short spurs, appearing just as the bronze-tinted new leaves are unfurling. Once established it tolerates the dry shade beneath mature trees; groom out winter-worn leaves in late winter to showcase the new season's flowers and foliage.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the narrow, spidery petals give this Sichuan species a distinctly airy, delicate look compared to broader-flowered epimediums.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, giving the clump a season or two to settle before it flowers at full display. Epimedium sutchuenense produces unusually narrow, thread-like yellow petals and sepals that give each flower a spidery, almost skeletal appearance, quite different from the broad-petaled look of most garden epimediums. Small, neat deciduous leaflets emerge with a faint bronze cast in spring and stay clean green through the growing season. Its restrained, clumping habit and unusual flower form make it a conversation piece for a shaded rock garden or collector's woodland border rather than a bulk groundcover.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; unlike most epimediums, this Yunnan and Guangxi species bears a single undivided, heart-shaped leaflet per leaf rather than the usual compound trio.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, where the clump spreads gently into a fine-textured groundcover. Epimedium simplicifolium is unusual among epimediums for its simple, undivided, heart-shaped leaflets, which give the foliage a softer, less angular texture than the compound leaves of most species in the genus. Small pink or white flowers with short spurs appear in spring on wiry stems held just above the mottled young foliage. Its low, spreading habit and distinctive leaf shape make it a useful textural contrast when planted alongside broader-leaved epimediums and hostas in a shaded border.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

common_name: Tama no Genpei Barrenwort (Bicolor Pink-and-White Longspur Epimedium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Japanese heirloom selection is named for the red-and-white banners of the historic Genpei War, since individual plants bear both pink and white flowers at once.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial or full shade, where the clump slowly thickens into a patch prized for its unusual flower display. Tama no Genpei is a long-cultivated Japanese selection of Epimedium grandiflorum that produces both pink and white flowers on the same plant, and often within the same cluster, in a pattern that can shift somewhat from year to year. Heart-shaped leaflets emerge tinged with bronze-red in spring before settling into soft green, providing an attractive backdrop to the bicolor blooms held on wiry stems. Because the pink-and-white pattern is an unstable, chimeral trait rather than a fixed genetic one, propagate only by division rather than seed to preserve the bicolor display.

common_name: Variegated Dwarf Solomon's Seal (Low Cream-Edged Running Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to full shade; this variegated sport of the dwarf running Solomon's seal stays much lower than the wide-margined odoratum and multiflorum cultivars usually grown for variegation.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in dappled or full shade, allowing room for the creeping rhizomes to spread into a low, dense mat. Unlike the taller, arching border Solomon's seals, this dwarf running species stays close to the ground, and this sport adds a crisp creamy-white edge to each narrow leaf along the wiry stems. Small, paired, greenish-white bell flowers dangle beneath the foliage in late spring, followed by dark berries in a good season. Because it spreads steadily by rhizome, use it as a slow-creeping variegated groundcover under shrubs or between larger woodland perennials rather than confining it to a tight border spot.
